title: Family and numbers
goal: Saying what you have and don't have with 有 / 冇, counting with classifiers, giving ages and phone numbers, and naming family members with the words Hongkongers actually use.
bekal: say you have something with 有 and don't have it with 冇
ask with 有冇 and answer
count with the pattern number + classifier + noun
tell 二 and 兩 apart
give ages, numbers of people, and phone numbers

dialogs.title: 對話 1 — A family photo
dialogs.intro: Wong Lai shows Andi a photo of her family. Notice that “have” and “not have” in Cantonese are two completely different words.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [呢張|Ni1 zoeng1][係|hai6][我屋企人|ngo5 uk1 kei2 jan4][嘅相|ge3 soeng2]。
lines.id: This is a photo of my family.
lines.literal: this — flat-classifier — is — my — home — person — possessive — photo.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [你屋企|Nei5 uk1 kei2][有|jau5][幾多人|gei2 do1 jan4][呀|aa3]？
lines.id: How many people are in your family?
lines.literal: you — home — have — how — many — person — huh.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [五個人|Ng5 go3 jan4]：[爸爸|baa4 baa1]、[媽媽|maa4 maa1]、[我|ngo5]，[同埋|tung4 maai4][兩個細佬|loeng5 go3 sai3 lou2]。
lines.id: Five: my dad, my mom, me, and two younger brothers.
lines.literal: five — classifier — person: dad, mom, me, and — two — classifier — younger-brother.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [你|Nei5][有冇|jau5 mou5][家姐|gaa1 ze1][呀|aa3]？
lines.id: Do you have an older sister?
lines.literal: you — have — not-have — older-sister — huh.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [冇|Mou5]，[我係|ngo5 hai6][大女|daai6 neoi2]。[你呢|Nei5 ne1]？
lines.id: No, I'm the eldest daughter. And you?
lines.literal: not-have, I — am — big — daughter. you — how-about.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [我有|Ngo5 jau5][一個家姐|jat1 go3 gaa1 ze1][同|tung4][一個細妹|jat1 go3 sai3 mui2]。
lines.id: I have one older sister and one younger sister.
lines.literal: I — have — one — classifier — older-sister — and — one — classifier — younger-sister.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [你細妹|Nei5 sai3 mui2][幾多歲|gei2 do1 seoi3][呀|aa3]？
lines.id: How old is your younger sister?
lines.literal: you — younger-sister — how — many — years-old — huh.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [佢十九歲|Keoi5 sap6 gau2 seoi3]，[仲讀緊書|zung6 duk6 gan2 syu1]。
lines.id: She's nineteen, still at university.
lines.literal: she — ten — nine — years-old, still — read — -ing — book.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [你爸爸媽媽|Nei5 baa4 baa1 maa4 maa1][喺印尼|hai2 Jan3 nei4][呀|aa3]？
lines.id: Are your parents in Indonesia?
lines.literal: you — dad — mom — at — Indonesia — huh.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [係呀|Hai6 aa3]，[佢哋喺|keoi5 dei6 hai2][雅加達|Ngaa5 gaa1 daat6]。
lines.id: Yes, they're in Jakarta.
lines.literal: is — yes, they — at — Jakarta.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [你掛唔掛住|Nei5 gwaa3 m4 gwaa3 zyu6][佢哋|keoi5 dei6][呀|aa3]？
lines.id: Do you miss them?
lines.literal: you — miss — not — miss — still — them — huh.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [梗係|Gang2 hai6][掛住|gwaa3 zyu6][啦|laa1]！
lines.id: Of course I do!
lines.literal: of-course — is — miss — still — sure.

notes: **⚠️ The opposite of [有|jau5] is [冇|mou5], not 唔有.** It's the only Cantonese verb negated with a different word instead of adding 唔. The form 唔有 doesn't exist at all — it sounds wrong instantly. Look at the characters too: 冇 is 有 with two strokes taken out, as if emptied.

**[屋企|uk1 kei2] means both “home” and “family”.** [我屋企|ngo5 uk1 kei2] = my home; [我屋企人|ngo5 uk1 kei2 jan4] = the people in my home, i.e. my family. ⚠️ This is a native Cantonese word — 家 appears in compounds but rarely stands alone the way 家 does in Mandarin.

**[張|zoeng1] is the classifier for flat things**: photos, paper, cards, tables, chairs, beds. [呢張相|ni1 zoeng1 soeng2] = this photo. A wrong classifier won't stop you being understood, but it instantly marks you as a foreigner.

**[嘅|ge3] is the possessive marker — Mandarin's 的.** [我嘅相|ngo5 ge3 soeng2] = my photo. 🇭🇰 But for very close possessions — family, body, home — 嘅 is actually **dropped**: [我屋企|ngo5 uk1 kei2], [我媽媽|ngo5 maa4 maa1], [你細妹|nei5 sai3 mui2]. Putting 嘅 there sounds distant.

**[家姐|gaa1 ze1] and [細佬|sai3 lou2] are everyday Hong Kong forms.** 🇭🇰 Textbooks teach 姐姐 and 弟弟, and they're understood — but what people really say is 家姐 (older sister), 大佬 *daai6 lou2* (older brother), 細佬 (younger brother), 細妹 *sai3 mui2* (younger sister).

**[仲|zung6] means “still” or “more”.** [佢仲讀緊書|Keoi5 zung6 duk6 gan2 syu1] = she's still in school. You'll see this word constantly, often paired with [未|mei6]: [仲未食|zung6 mei6 sik6] = still haven't eaten.

**[梗係…啦|Gang2 hai6 … laa1] = “of course!”.** A very Cantonese paired pattern: 梗係 in front, 啦 at the end. It answers questions whose answer is obvious. [梗係要啦|Gang2 hai6 jiu3 laa1]！ = of course I want it!

grammars.title: 有 / 冇 — have, there is, and how to ask
body: [有|jau5] covers two meanings at once, like “have” and “there is” in English: **owning** something, and something **existing** somewhere.
The question uses the A-唔-A pattern you already know — but in a special form, since the negative isn't 唔有 but 冇: **有冇**.

head: Form
Example
Meaning
rows: [我有兩個細佬|Ngo5 jau5 loeng5 go3 sai3 lou2]。
I don't have an older sister.
[你有冇仔女呀|Nei5 jau5 mou5 zai2 neoi2 aa3]？

after: **[冇|mou5] is also used for “didn't” and “haven't”.** [我冇去|Ngo5 mou5 heoi3] = I didn't go (that time). 🔁 How it differs from [唔去|m4 heoi3] (won't go, don't want to go) is sorted out in Unit 9.
⚠️ **Don't use Mandarin 沒有.** In Hong Kong it sounds like reading a newspaper. One syllable, 冇, covers everything.

grammars.title: Number + classifier + noun
body: Cantonese never attaches a number directly to a noun. A **classifier** always stands between them — a bit like *a cup of*, *a sheet of*, *a head of* in English, but required every single time.

head: Classifier
Used for
Example
rows: people and general things — if unsure, use this
flat things: photos, paper, tables, cards
[一部電話|jat1 bou6 din6 waa2] one phone
rooms and buildings: shops, houses, schools
[三間舖頭|saam1 gaan1 pou3 tau2] three shops

head: Pattern
Example
Meaning
rows: the phone (the one we know about)

after: **⚠️ The number “two” has two forms, and they can't be swapped.** [二|ji6] is only for counting, numbers, dates, and inside larger numbers. [兩|loeng5] is used whenever the number stands before a classifier. So: [兩個人|loeng5 go3 jan4] (two people), but [二十|ji6 sap6] (twenty) and [十二號|sap6 ji6 hou6] (number twelve).
**A classifier with no number means “the”.** [部電話壞咗|Bou6 din6 waa2 waai6 zo2] = the phone's broken — the phone we've been talking about. It does the job of the English article, and it's very common.
🔁 **The full classifier list is in the summary at the back of the book.** For now, master 個 and 張 first; together they cover most everyday conversation.

dialogs.title: 對話 2 — Children, ages, and phone numbers
dialogs.intro: Andi meets Mr. Chan again. This conversation is number practice disguised as small talk — read the numbers out loud, don't skip them.

lines.speaker: 陳生:
lines.text: [你有冇|Nei5 jau5 mou5][仔女|zai2 neoi2][呀|aa3]？
lines.id: Do you have children?
lines.literal: you — have — not-have — son — daughter — huh.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [冇|Mou5]，[我仲未|ngo5 zung6 mei6][結婚|git3 fan1]。
lines.id: Not yet, I'm not married yet.
lines.literal: not-have, I — still — not-yet — tie — marriage.

lines.speaker: 陳生:
lines.text: [我有|Ngo5 jau5][兩個仔|loeng5 go3 zai2]，[一個女|jat1 go3 neoi2]。
lines.id: I have two sons and a daughter.
lines.literal: I — have — two — classifier — son, one — classifier — daughter.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [佢哋|Keoi5 dei6][幾多歲|gei2 do1 seoi3][呀|aa3]？
lines.id: How old are they?
lines.literal: they — how — many — years-old — huh.

lines.speaker: 陳生:
lines.text: [大仔|Daai6 zai2][十二歲|sap6 ji6 seoi3]，[細仔|sai3 zai2][九歲|gau2 seoi3]，[個女|go3 neoi2][得四歲|dak1 sei3 seoi3]。
lines.id: The older boy is twelve, the younger one nine, and my daughter is only four.
lines.literal: big — son — twelve — years, small — son — nine — years, classifier — daughter — only — four — years.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [好熱鬧|Hou2 jit6 naau6][喎|wo3]！
lines.id: Wow, what a lively family!
lines.literal: filler — lively — you-know.

lines.speaker: 陳生:
lines.text: [係呀|Hai6 aa3]，[屋企|uk1 kei2][成日|seng4 jat6][好嘈|hou2 cou4]。
lines.id: Yes, the house is noisy all day.
lines.literal: is — yes, home — whole — day — filler — noisy.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [唔該|M4 goi1][畀|bei2][你個電話號碼|nei5 go3 din6 waa2 hou6 maa5][我|ngo5]。
lines.id: Could I have your phone number?
lines.literal: please — give — you — classifier — phone — number — me.

lines.speaker: 陳生:
lines.text: [九八七六|Gau2 baat3 cat1 luk6][五四三二|ng5 sei3 saam1 ji6]。
lines.literal: nine — eight — seven — six — five — four — three — two.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [等等|Dang2 dang2]，[你講|nei5 gong2][快咗啲|faai3 zo2 di1]…[唔該|m4 goi1][講慢啲|gong2 maan6 di1]。
lines.id: Wait, you're talking a bit fast… please slow down.
lines.literal: wait — wait, you — speak — fast — already — a-bit … please — speak — slow — a-bit.

lines.speaker: 陳生:
lines.text: [哈哈|Haa1 haa1]，[九|gau2] — [八|baat3] — [七|cat1] — [六|luk6] — [五|ng5] — [四|sei3] — [三|saam1] — [二|ji6]。
lines.id: Haha — nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two.
lines.literal: ha — ha, nine — eight — seven — six — five — four — three — two.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [多謝晒|Do1 ze6 saai3]！
lines.id: Thanks so much!
lines.literal: many — thanks — completely.

notes: **[仔女|zai2 neoi2] = children, combining [仔|zai2] (son) and [女|neoi2] (daughter).** Note the tone of 女: its dictionary form is *neoi5*, but people say *neoi2* — this is the changed tone explained in the opening chapter.

**[得|dak1] in [得四歲|dak1 sei3 seoi3] means “only”.** It goes before an amount to show the amount is small. [得十蚊|dak1 sap6 man1] = only ten dollars. 🔁 The same word also means “can / OK”, covered in Unit 10.

**Phone numbers are read digit by digit, not as one big number.** 9876 is read [九八七六|gau2 baat3 cat1 luk6], not “nine thousand eight hundred…”. 🇭🇰 Hong Kong phone numbers always have eight digits, and people read them in two groups of four.

**⚠️ One and seven sound alike to beginners' ears: [一|jat1] and [七|cat1].** The only difference is the first sound, and both are tone 1. When giving phone numbers, Hongkongers often stress 七 by raising their voice slightly. Practice this pair until you can tell them apart without thinking.
**[晒|saai3] means “all, completely, entirely”.** [多謝晒|Do1 ze6 saai3] = thanks so much. [食晒|Sik6 saai3] = eat it all up. It always attaches after the verb. 🔁 Covered fully in Unit 9.
**[成日|seng4 jat6] literally means “the whole day”, but it means “always, all the time”.** [佢成日遲到|Keoi5 seng4 jat6 ci4 dou3] = he's always late. Not literally all day long.

**[畀|bei2] = give, and the word order differs from English.** Cantonese pattern: 畀 + thing + person. [畀本書我|Bei2 bun2 syu1 ngo5] = give me the book — the thing first, the recipient last. ⚠️ This is the reverse of Mandarin 給我一本書 and of English “give me the book”, and it's where learners trip up most.

grammars.title: Ages, numbers of people, and how to ask “how many”
body: Cantonese has two words for “how many”, and your choice depends on how big you expect the number to be.

head: Word
Used when
Example
rows: you expect a small answer (under ten)
[你有幾個仔|Nei5 jau5 gei2 go3 zai2]？ How many sons do you have?
the answer could be large, or you can't guess
[你屋企有幾多人|Nei5 uk1 kei2 jau5 gei2 do1 jan4]？ How many people are in your family?

head: Question
Answer
rows: [你幾多歲呀|Nei5 gei2 do1 seoi3 aa3]？ (to an adult)
[你幾歲呀|Nei5 gei2 seoi3 aa3]？ (to a small child)
[你電話幾多號呀|Nei5 din6 waa2 gei2 do1 hou6 aa3]？
[九八七六五四三二|Gau2 baat3 cat1 luk6 ng5 sei3 saam1 ji6]。
[你哋幾多位呀|Nei5 dei6 gei2 do1 wai2 aa3]？ (at a restaurant)

after: **Notice that age does NOT use 係.** [我三十歲|Ngo5 saam1 sap6 seoi3] — no verb at all. Slipping 係 in is wrong: 我係三十歲 sounds like “I am the thirty years”.
🇭🇰 **At restaurants, people are counted with [位|wai2], not 個.** The waiter asks [幾多位|gei2 do1 wai2]？ and you answer [兩位|loeng5 wai2] — the politeness is built into the classifier.

sections.title: Numbers: from zero to ten thousand

blocks.text: Cantonese numbers work like a machine: once you know one to ten, all the rest build themselves without a single irregular form.
Eleven to nineteen = **十 + unit**. Tens = **digit + 十**, then the unit tacked on the end.

blocks.title: Four things that will save you with numbers
items: ⚠️ **二 vs 兩 once more**, because it's the number-one mistake: [二|ji6] for counting and numbers; [兩|loeng5] before a classifier. [二十二|ji6 sap6 ji6] (twenty-two) but [兩個|loeng5 go3] (two of them).

🇭🇰 **Large numbers are grouped by ten thousands, not thousands.** [一萬|jat1 maan6] = 10,000, [十萬|sap6 maan6] = 100,000, [一百萬|jat1 baak3 maan6] = 1,000,000. This is where people get lost when talking about house prices and salaries.
**[半|bun3] = half**, placed where the number goes: [一個半鐘|jat1 go3 bun3 zung1] = an hour and a half.
**Zero is read [零|ling4] only inside a number**: 105 = [一百零五|jat1 baak3 ling4 ng5]. In phone numbers, 0 is also read [零|ling4] — some people say *o*, like the English letter O.

sections.title: The Hong Kong family: written forms and spoken forms

blocks.text: Cantonese distinguishes older and younger siblings, and the father's side from the mother's side. The right-hand column is what you'll actually hear in Hong Kong — that's the one to learn first.

blocks.title: Three things to know about family
items: ⚠️ **[老豆|lou5 dau6] and [老母|lou5 mou2] are affectionate, not rude — but only for your own parents.** Using them for someone else's parents sounds impolite. For that, use [你爸爸|nei5 baa4 baa1] or the very formal [令尊|ling6 zyun1].

**There's no single word for “siblings”.** Instead people use the string [兄弟姊妹|hing1 dai6 zi2 mui6] — older brother, younger brother, older sister, younger sister all at once. [你有冇兄弟姊妹呀|Nei5 jau5 mou5 hing1 dai6 zi2 mui6 aa3]？ = do you have any brothers or sisters?

🇭🇰 **[阿|aa3] goes in front of a family term or name to sound affectionate**: [阿媽|aa3 maa1] (mom), [阿哥|aa3 go1] (big brother), [阿麗|Aa3 Lai6] (our Lai). It's a very Cantonese habit that Mandarin doesn't have.

exercises.prompt: Correct these wrong sentences, then write the right version in Jyutping.
items: [我唔有家姐|Ngo5 m4 jau5 gaa1 ze1]。
[我有二個仔|Ngo5 jau5 ji6 go3 zai2]。
[我係三十歲|Ngo5 hai6 saam1 sap6 seoi3]。

answers: 有 — 冇 — 冇 — 有 — 冇 — 有
兩 — 二 — 兩 — 二 — 兩
我 有 兩 個 細佬 — 你 屋企 有 幾多 人 — 佢 冇 家姐 — 我 細妹 十九 歲 — 唔該 畀 你 電話 我 — 佢哋 都 喺 印尼
There are five people in my family. — His daughter is only four. — Do you have any brothers or sisters? — I'm not married yet. — They're always noisy.
Ngo5 jau5 loeng5 go3 sai3 lou2. — Ngo5 mou5 gaa1 ze1. — Nei5 sai3 mui2 gei2 do1 seoi3 aa3? — Nei5 uk1 kei2 jau5 gei2 do1 jan4 aa3? — M4 goi1 bei2 nei5 go3 din6 waa2 hou6 maa5 ngo5.
Ngo5 mou5 gaa1 ze1. — Ngo5 jau5 loeng5 go3 zai2. — Ngo5 saam1 sap6 seoi3. — Ngo5 jau5 loeng5 go3 zai2. — M4 goi1 bei2 bun2 syu1 ngo5.
wave: Five minutes before Unit 3: draw your own family tree on a sheet of paper, then write the Cantonese term next to each person — use the “what people say” column, not the written-form column. Then say each person's age out loud in a full sentence: [我爸爸六十二歲|Ngo5 baa4 baa1 luk6 sap6 ji6 seoi3]。 Numbers used for real people stick far faster than numbers memorized from a list.
